exercises.name: Abs
setup: On your back, arms straight up, hips and knees at ninety degrees.
Press the lower back gently into the floor and keep it there.
execution: Lower the opposite arm and leg towards the floor, slowly.
Stop the moment the lower back starts to lift, return, and swap sides.
cues: The lower back staying flat is the whole exercise.
Breathe out slowly as the limbs move away.
Slower is harder - there is no need to add weight for a long time.

mistakes.mistake: Lower back arching off the floor
mistakes.fix: Shorten the range; only go as far as the back stays down.
Three seconds out, three back. Speed hides the work.
Exhale on the way out - breathing under brace is the skill.

exercises.breathing: Long exhale as the limbs extend, inhale coming back.

evidence.claim: Anti-movement core work transfers well
evidence.detail: Bracing against motion - planks, dead bugs, Pallof presses - builds trunk stiffness that carries into squats and carries.

evidence.claim: Loaded flexion does grow the abs
evidence.detail: Cable crunches and hanging raises add size; they simply load the spine more than anti-extension work.

evidence.claim: Visible abs are mostly a body-fat question
evidence.detail: Training grows the muscle; whether it shows is decided in the kitchen.

progressions: Add a light dumbbell in the hands
regressions: Feet on the floor between reps

exercises.name: Back
setup: Hinge at the hips until the torso is around 45 degrees, back flat.
Arms hanging straight, shoulder blades relaxed forward.
execution: Pull the elbows back and slightly in, bringing the bar to the lower ribs.
Let the shoulder blades travel apart again at the bottom - do not just move the arms.
cues: Lead with the elbows, not the hands.
Think of the arms as hooks; the back does the pulling.
Let the weight stretch you at the bottom.

mistakes.fix: The angle should stay put. If it does not, the weight is too heavy.

mistakes.mistake: Pulling to the chest instead of the ribs
mistakes.fix: High pulls turn it into a rear-delt exercise - fine, but a different one.
Allow the shoulder blades to move; that is where the lats lengthen.

exercises.breathing: Brace at the top of the rep, exhale as you finish the pull.

evidence.claim: Rowing and pulling down are not the same exercise
evidence.detail: Horizontal and vertical pulls emphasise different parts of the back; a complete back needs both.

evidence.claim: Chest support removes the lower-back limit
evidence.detail: If the erectors fatigue before the back does, a supported row lets you train the target muscle harder.

evidence.claim: Grip is often the first thing to fail
evidence.detail: Straps let the back reach failure instead of the hands, which is the point of the set.

progressions: Pause one second at the ribs

exercises.name: Biceps
setup: Stand tall, arms hanging, palms forward, elbows just in front of the ribs.
Shoulders back and down; the upper arm is going to stay still.
execution: Curl by bending the elbow only, until the forearm is past vertical.
Lower all the way until the arm is straight - the bottom is not a rest stop.
cues: Pin the elbow to your side like it is hinged there.
Lower for a count of three; the lowering is half the exercise.
Straighten the arm fully at the bottom before the next rep.

mistakes.mistake: Swinging the torso to start the rep
mistakes.fix: Stand with your back against a wall for a set - if you cannot cheat, the weight is honest.
Keep the upper arm vertical so the biceps, not the front delt, does the work.
Let the arm straighten; the stretched position builds the most.

evidence.claim: Training a muscle in its stretched position pays off
evidence.detail: Work that loads the muscle long - incline curls for the biceps - tends to produce more growth than the same sets done short.

evidence.claim: Full range beats partial range for growth
evidence.detail: Moving through the whole range generally outgrows cutting the ends off, with the lengthened half doing most of the work.

evidence.claim: Small muscles recover fast
evidence.detail: Arms tolerate and often benefit from more frequent work than the big compound lifts.

progressions: Incline bench curl for a deeper stretch
Add weight when 12 reps feel easy
regressions: Seated curl to stop the swing

exercises.name: Calves
alternatives: Single-leg calf raise on a step
setup: Balls of the feet on a step, heels hanging free, knees straight for the gastroc.
Hold something for balance - this is not a balance exercise.
execution: Drop the heels below the step until you feel a deep stretch.
Rise as high as the joint allows and hold the top for a second.
cues: Pause a full second at the bottom - no bouncing.
Go all the way up onto the big toe, not the little toe.
Straight knee trains the calf; bent knee trains the soleus underneath it.

mistakes.fix: The Achilles springs you up and the muscle does nothing. Pause.
Rise until the ankle cannot go further, then hold.
Add a seated version - the soleus is most of the calf's size.

evidence.claim: Calves need full range and a pause to grow
evidence.detail: The stretched position with the heel below the step is where the work happens; bouncing hands the job to the tendon.

evidence.claim: Straight-leg and bent-leg work hit different muscles
evidence.detail: Standing raises bias the gastrocnemius, seated raises the soleus - training both covers the whole calf.

evidence.claim: Calves tolerate higher reps well
evidence.detail: They handle frequent, higher-rep work, though the usual effort rule still applies.

regressions: Flat floor instead of a step

exercises.name: Hamstrings
setup: Stand with the weight at the top of the thighs, feet hip width, knees softly bent.
Shoulders back, bar close, weight through the middle of the foot.
execution: Push the hips back and let the torso fold forward, keeping the back flat.
Stop when you feel a strong stretch behind the thighs - usually mid-shin.
Drive the hips forward to stand, squeezing the glutes at the top.
cues: Hips back, not down - this is a hinge, not a squat.
Drag the bar down your legs; it should stay in contact.
Stop where your hamstrings stop you, not where the floor is.

mistakes.mistake: Rounding the lower back to reach further
mistakes.fix: Range comes from the hips. Stop at the point where the back would round.
Keep the shin close to vertical; the knee angle barely changes.
Finish standing tall with the glutes squeezed, not hyperextended.

exercises.breathing: Big breath at the top, hold it through the rep, exhale after standing up.

evidence.claim: Hamstrings respond to both hip-hinge and knee-flexion work
evidence.detail: The two halves of the muscle are trained differently - an RDL and a leg curl are not interchangeable, and doing both covers more.

evidence.claim: Lengthened-position work is especially effective here
evidence.detail: Exercises that load the hamstring long, like RDLs and Nordics, show strong growth and a protective effect against strains.

evidence.claim: Eccentric-focused hamstring work reduces strain risk
evidence.detail: Programmes built around slow lowering, notably Nordic curls, are among the better supported injury-prevention findings in sport.

progressions: Pause two seconds in the stretch
Add load once form holds for 10 reps
regressions: Dumbbell RDL with a shorter range
Seated leg curl if the lower back complains

exercises.name: Jumping jacks
setup: Stand tall, feet together, arms at the sides.
Land softly - think quiet feet.
execution: Jump the feet apart while the arms sweep overhead.
Jump back to the start. Keep a steady rhythm rather than a sprint.
cues: Land on the middle of the foot, knees soft.
Arms all the way overhead, not to shoulder height.
Breathe in a rhythm you could hold for two minutes.

mistakes.fix: Let the knees and ankles absorb it - quiet feet.
Full overhead makes it a warm-up for the shoulders too.
This is a warm-up or a conditioning filler; pace it.

evidence.claim: A general warm-up raises muscle temperature and performance
evidence.detail: A few minutes of easy whole-body movement before lifting improves force output and feels better than going in cold.

evidence.claim: Easy cardio adds up without eating into recovery
evidence.detail: Low-intensity work like this and walking builds a base with little interference with strength training.

evidence.claim: Impact tolerance builds gradually
evidence.detail: If knees or shins complain, step jacks give most of the benefit without the landing.

regressions: Step jacks, one foot at a time

exercises.name: Lats
setup: Grip a little wider than the shoulders, arms fully straight, ribs down.
Start from a dead hang - shoulders long, not shrugged into the ears.
execution: Pull the elbows down and into the ribs until the chin clears the bar or the bar reaches the collarbone.
Lower all the way back to straight arms under control.
cues: Pull your elbows into your back pockets.
Chest up to meet the bar.
Full hang at the bottom, every rep.

mistakes.fix: The stretch at the bottom is where the lats grow. Let the arms straighten.

mistakes.mistake: Kipping to get the chin over
mistakes.fix: Use assistance or a pulldown and keep it strict.
Start the rep by pulling the shoulder blades down.

exercises.breathing: Exhale pulling up, inhale on the way down.

evidence.claim: A full hang builds more lat than a short pull
evidence.detail: The bottom of the movement loads the lats in their longest position, which is where most of the growth comes from.

evidence.claim: Pulldowns and pull-ups build the same muscle
evidence.detail: If strict pull-ups are out of reach, a pulldown taken close to failure does the job.

evidence.claim: Wider is not automatically better
evidence.detail: Grip width changes comfort more than it changes lat recruitment; use the width your shoulders like.

exercises.name: Push-ups
setup: Hands just wider than the shoulders, under the collarbones rather than the face.
Body in one line from ear to ankle, glutes and quads switched on.
execution: Lower until the chest is about a fist off the floor, elbows at roughly 45 degrees.
Press back up and push the floor away at the top.
cues: Squeeze the glutes - it turns the plank into a press.
Elbows at 45 degrees, not flared to the sides.
Push the floor away at the top and let the shoulder blades spread.

mistakes.fix: Brace the ribs down and squeeze the glutes; raise the hands if the plank cannot hold.

mistakes.mistake: Head reaching for the floor first
mistakes.fix: The chest should arrive first; keep the neck neutral.
Hard on the shoulder and weaker. Tuck to about 45.

exercises.breathing: Inhale on the way down, exhale pressing up.

evidence.claim: Bodyweight pressing builds chest when taken near failure
evidence.detail: With enough reps and proximity to failure, push-ups produce growth comparable to bench pressing at matched effort.

evidence.claim: Load can be added without a gym
evidence.detail: Elevating the feet, slowing the lowering or adding a pack keeps push-ups in a productive rep range as you get stronger.

evidence.claim: Range matters as much here as anywhere
evidence.detail: A chest-to-fist depth beats a half rep; deficit push-ups extend the range further.

regressions: Hands on a bench or wall

exercises.name: Quads
setup: Feet between hip and shoulder width, toes slightly out.
Brace as if about to be pushed, whole foot planted.
execution: Sit down and slightly back, letting the knees travel forward over the toes.
Descend until the hip crease is at least level with the knee, if your hips allow it.
Drive up through the whole foot, keeping the chest angle the same.
cues: Knees out over the middle toes, not collapsing in.
Spread the floor with your feet on the way up.
Keep the bar over the middle of the foot the whole way.

mistakes.fix: Ankle mobility or a too-wide stance. Try shoes with a heel, or squat to a slightly higher depth.
The chest and hips should rise together; lighten the load until they do.
Depth is where the quads earn it - go as deep as you can with a flat back.

exercises.breathing: Breath in and brace at the top, hold through the rep, exhale at the top.

evidence.claim: Deeper squats build more quad and glute than shallow ones
evidence.detail: At matched load, greater depth produces more growth in the thigh - quarter squats mostly build the ability to do quarter squats.

evidence.claim: Three minutes of rest beats one on the big lifts
evidence.detail: Longer rests preserve reps across sets, and total hard reps is what drives the adaptation.

evidence.claim: Machines and free weights both work
evidence.detail: If a leg press or split squat lets you train hard with less fatigue or discomfort, it is not a downgrade.

regressions: Box squat to a comfortable depth

exercises.name: Shoulders
setup: Sit or stand tall, dumbbells at shoulder height, palms facing forward or slightly in.
Ribs down, glutes and core braced so the lower back does not arch.
execution: Press the weights up and slightly back until the arms are straight overhead.
Lower under control until the elbows are level with, or just below, the shoulders.
cues: Press the dumbbells around your head, not in front of it.
Squeeze the glutes - it stops the lower back from taking the load.
Finish with the biceps beside the ears, not in front of the face.

mistakes.mistake: Lower back arching to help the press
mistakes.fix: Lighten the load and brace the ribs down; sit with back support if it keeps happening.
Lower until the elbow is at shoulder height - the stretched position is where most of the growth comes from.
Let the shoulder blades rotate naturally but keep the traps from doing the work.

exercises.breathing: Inhale at the top or on the way down, brace, exhale as you press through the hard part.

evidence.claim: Effort matters more than the exact rep number
evidence.detail: Sets taken within a few reps of failure grow muscle across a wide rep range - roughly 5 to 30 reps - so pick a weight you can control and stop 1-3 reps short.

evidence.claim: Around 10-20 hard sets per muscle per week is the usual sweet spot
evidence.detail: Dose-response work on weekly set volume shows more sets keep helping up to a point, after which returns flatten and fatigue costs rise.

evidence.claim: Two sessions a week beats one at the same total volume
evidence.detail: Spreading the same number of sets over two days tends to edge out cramming them into one.

progressions: Add 2.5 kg once you hit the top of the rep range with two reps in reserve
Single-arm press for more core demand
regressions: Landmine press if overhead is uncomfortable

exercises.name: Sit-ups
setup: Knees bent, feet flat, hands across the chest rather than behind the head.
Chin lightly tucked.
execution: Curl the spine up one vertebra at a time until the torso is off the floor.
Lower with the same control - do not drop back.
cues: Roll up, do not hinge up in one plank-like piece.
Hands on the chest; pulling on the neck is just cheating.
Lower slower than you rise.

mistakes.fix: Cross the arms over the chest instead.
If the lower back arches or the feet lift, switch to crunches or dead bugs.
Pause a beat at the bottom.

evidence.claim: Sit-ups do train the abs, and they also load the spine
evidence.detail: Repeated loaded flexion is a known contributor to disc stress; if your back objects, crunches or anti-extension work get the same muscle with less of it.

evidence.claim: There is no such thing as spot reduction
evidence.detail: Abdominal training does not preferentially burn abdominal fat.

evidence.claim: Adding load beats adding reps forever
evidence.detail: Once you can do 25 clean reps, a cable crunch or a held plate progresses the muscle better than doubling the count.

progressions: Hold a plate on the chest

plans.name: Five mornings, whole body
plans.summary: Built around the eleven things you tick in the gym. Five short sessions, each muscle trained twice a week, treadmill as the warm-up and the filler.
notes: Every set stops one to three reps short of failure. That is the dial that matters.
Add a little weight, or a rep, whenever you hit the top of the rep range twice in a row.
If you get four sessions in instead of five, drop Friday, not Monday.

days.title: Push
days.warmup: Treadmill 8 min, then jumping jacks x 30

targets.note: Protein target is roughly 1.6 g per kg for a 80 kg body - the range the literature settles on for building muscle. Calories are a starting point: adjust by how the weight trend moves over a fortnight, not day to day.
